Rails' `params` (specifically `params[:order]`) is a user-controlled hash — any key the attacker adds gets passed straight into `Order.new`/`update` if you hand the raw hash over, which is mass assignment. (or on older Rails: `params.require(:order).permit(:product_id, :quantity, :shipping_address_id)`)

- Keep the action thin: params in, call the model or a service object, render/redirect out. If creating an order spans multiple models, calls a payment provider, etc., extract a service object rather than piling it into `create`.

    redirect_to @order, notice: "Order created"
  else
    render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
  end

private

def order_params

# Handling params in an Orders `create` action

Don't pass `params[:order]` straight into `Order.new`/`Order.create` — that mass-assigns *every* key in the hash, including ones the form never should have been able to set (an `:admin`, `:user_id`, `:status`, `:total` field, etc.). Anyone can add a field to the form POST and set it. Always go through strong parameters.

## The permitted shape

Current Rails idiom:

```ruby
# app/controllers/orders_controller.rb
class OrdersController < ApplicationController
  before_action :authenticate_user!   # whatever this app's auth filter is

  def create
    order = current_user.orders.build(order_params)
    if order.save
      redirect_to order, notice: "Order created."
    else
      render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end
  end

  private

  def order_params
    params.expect(order: [:product_id, :quantity, :shipping_address])
  end
end
```

On older Rails (pre-`expect`), the equivalent is:

```ruby
params.require(:order).permit(:product_id, :quantity, :shipping_address)
```

Two things to note:

1. **Name the fields explicitly.** Every attribute the form should be able to set gets listed; nothing else gets through. If a new field is added to the model later, it is *not* silently settable from the form until someone adds it here — that's the point.
2. **Never `permit!`** on params that came from a user. It disables the whole protection and mass-assigns anything.

## Don't trust client-supplied identity/ownership fields

Even with strong parameters, don't accept `user_id`, `account_id`, `status`, or a computed `total` from the form. Derive them server-side:

```ruby
# good: ownership from the session, not from params
order = current_user.orders.build(order_params)

# good: price/status computed, not submitted
```

If `current_user.orders.build(...)` is how ownership is set, then `:user_id` never needs to be in the permit list at all — which is the safest possible answer.

## When "just save the form fields" needs a service object

If the create action is more than "build from permitted params and save" — e.g. it also reserves inventory, charges a payment method, or sends a confirmation — don't stack that into the controller action or a model callback. Keep the controller thin and hand the orchestration to a service object, passing it already-permitted, already-trusted values:

```ruby
# app/controllers/orders_controller.rb
def create
  result = PlaceOrder.call(user: current_user, attributes: order_params)

  if result.success?
    redirect_to result.order, notice: "Order placed."
  else
    @order = result.order
    render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity
  end
end

private

def order_params
  params.expect(order: [:product_id, :quantity, :shipping_address])
end
```

```ruby
# app/services/place_order.rb
class PlaceOrder
  Result = Data.define(:success?, :order) do
    def success? = @success   # endless method for a real one-liner
  end

  def self.call(...) = new(...).call

  def initialize(user:, attributes:)
    @user = user
    @attributes = attributes
  end

  def call
    order = @user.orders.build(@attributes)
    order.total = Pricing.total_for(order)

    if order.save
      ChargeCardJob.perform_later(order.id)   # make this job idempotent
      Result.new(success?: true, order: order)
    else
      Result.new(success?: false, order: order)
    end
  end
end
```

The key boundary: **strong parameters happens in the controller**, before anything else touches the hash. The service object receives a hash that is already known-safe, so it never has to re-decide what's user-settable.

- [ ] Controller action goes through `params.expect(order: [...])` or `require`+`permit`; no `permit!`.
- [ ] `:user_id`/ownership is derived from `current_user`, not from params.
- [ ] Computed fields (`total`, `status`) are set server-side, not permitted.
- [ ] If the action does more than build-and-save, that logic lives in a service object, not the controller or a model callback.
- [ ] Any job fired from here is safe to run more than once (Rails queues are at-least-once).
- [ ] `bundle exec rspec` and `bundle exec rubocop` pass before you call it done.

`db:test:prepare` loads the test database from `db/schema.rb`. A migration that failed partway through means one of two things happened:

2. The migration partially committed (some adapters/DDL can't be rolled back cleanly), so the *dev* DB has a half-applied index definition while `db/schema.rb` reflects only the last *successful* `db:migrate` run.

**1. Find out what actually applied.**

```bash

```

On PostgreSQL, `add_index ..., algorithm: :concurrently` **cannot run inside a transaction** — if the migration is transactional (the default) it will raise `PG::ActiveSqlTransaction: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block`.
